slides.headline: An estimated 650 adult gharials remain in the wild.
slides.sub: A crocodile built for fish, running out of river

slides.headline: A snout built for fish
slides.body: Long, narrow jaws lined with sharp, interlocking teeth strike quickly at fish. Adults eat mainly fish; young gharials also take insects, crustaceans and frogs.

slides.headline: The pot on his nose
slides.body: Adult males grow a bulb on the snout tip called a ghara, after an Indian pot. It resonates their buzzing calls and signals to females. (Captive male pictured.)

slides.label: mature gharials left in the wild (best estimate 650)
slides.body: Critically Endangered on the IUCN Red List (assessed 2017). It is already extinct in Pakistan, Bhutan and Myanmar.

slides.headline: Rivers cut into pieces
slides.body: Dams and diversions split its rivers, mining and quarrying damage them, and overfishing takes its food. Weak on land, it cannot easily move to new rivers.
slides.source: IUCN Red List; Smithsonian's National Zoo

slides.headline: Saved once, still not safe
slides.body: Gharials nearly vanished in the 1970s. Despite breeding and release programmes, numbers fell 58% from 1997 to 2006. IUCN now lists the trend as increasing.
slides.source: Smithsonian's National Zoo; IUCN Red List

caption:
The gharial (Gavialis gangeticus) is a fish-eating crocodile with an estimated 650 adults left in the wild.

Its range once ran through the rivers of six countries, from Pakistan to Myanmar. Today wild gharials survive in fragmented stretches of river, mainly in northern India and Nepal, and the species is Critically Endangered. Females dig their nests in sandbanks in the dry season and lay an average of 40 eggs.

Swipe for the snout, the ghara and the threats. Sources on the last slide.

Source: IUCN Red List (Gavialis gangeticus, assessed 2017); Smithsonian's National Zoo.

Save this for the next time someone calls every crocodile the same.
